content: The agent recognized that the Dung AF is a sharp projection of the Model rather than the whole graph: dung_extensions operates only on argument→argument Attack relations, ignoring statement-level attacks and undercuts.
rationale: After exploring the dung_extensions contract the agent wrote: 'it operates only on argument→argument attack relations (`<X>\n - <Y>`) — statement-level attacks and undercuts are ignored. So the Dung AF is a sharp projection of the Model, not the whole graph.'

content: @argdown/core dung_extensions counts only argument→argument Attack edges; a 3-argument attack chain A→B→C yields grounded {A,C} IN, {B} OUT, and a statement-level relation reference is rejected as invalid premise/conclusion content.
rationale: Probe of a 3-arg chain returned 'Grounded extension: 2 IN, 1 OUT' with {A,C} in / {B} out; a `><` contradictory probe returned a parse error 'An argument reference (<Argument Title>) ... can not be used as premise or conclusion within a premise-conclusion-structure.'

content: The reference does NOT promote a `{tags: [...]}` metadata key into entity tags by default — only inline #tags landed in the argument's tags list — so 'tags-promotion' is config-gated and a candidate to defer.
rationale: export_json probe of `<Arg>: an argument #foo {tags: [meta-tag, foo]}` produced `tags: ["foo"]` (only the inline #foo), not the metadata-key values. Agent concluded: 'a `{tags: [...]}` metadata key was NOT promoted by default ... so "tags-promotion" looks config-gated, a candidate to defer.'

content: The reference builds a top-level tags registry keyed by tag name with first-occurrence ordering ({tag, cssClass, occurrenceIndex}), and each statement/argument carries its own tags list, all sourced from inline #tags.
rationale: export_json output showed a `tags` object keyed by name with `occurrenceIndex: 0/1` and `cssClass: tag-foo`, plus per-entity `tags: [...]` arrays. Agent summarized this shape and modeled B6a's registry on it (dropping cssClass).

content: The agent allocated process effort by risk: B6a (tags) built directly as mechanical like B4a, while B6b (the cross-cutting AF/extension) got a chorus brain-jam, run in the background while B6a was built.
rationale: Agent: 'B6a (tags) is mechanical like B4a — I'll build it directly. B6b (the cross-cutting AF/extension) gets the chorus. Let me kick off the B6b brain-jam in the background (it takes ~10 min) and build B6a while it runs.'

content: B6a models tags as Tags { tags: Vec<String> (first-occurrence order), block_tags: Vec<Vec<TagId>> } index-aligned with document.blocks, deferring per-equivalence-class aggregation to keep the slice thin and avoid re-deriving the B3/B4 registries.
rationale: Spec Decision 3: 'B6a's block_tags is per-block, not per-entity; a consumer composes it with B3/B4a's block→entity maps ... Keeping B6a per-block avoids re-deriving the registries and keeps the slice thin.' Mirrors the project's index-aligned-Vec template (block_sections/block_statements/block_pcs).

content: The chorus surfaced a load-bearing disagreement: the skeptic argued B5 emits Node::Statement endpoints for relations nested under PCS premises, so the sharp argument→argument filter would silently drop every nested attack, and proposed a StatementMapper to lift statements to their containing argument.
rationale: Agent: 'the architect says sharp projection ... matches the reference; the skeptic insists B5 emits Node::Statement endpoints for relations nested under PCS premises, so the filter would silently drop them ... These diverge on a critical point ... the stakes (empty AF vs correct AF) demand a probe.'

content: Probe settled the chorus debate: an argument-level `<a>\n - <b>` yields 1 attack with grounded {b IN, a OUT} (so `-` means the target attacks the parent), while the same attack nested under a PCS premise yields 0 attacks — the reference ignores statement-level attacks, vindicating the sharp projection over the skeptic's StatementMapper.
rationale: Two probes: P1 (argument-level) → '1 IN, 1 OUT ... in:[b], out:[a]'; P2 (statement-level under PCS premise) → '2 IN, 0 OUT ... 0 attacks'. Agent: 'the sharp projection is reference-correct ... The skeptic's StatementMapper would over-count and diverge from the reference — rejected.'

content: B6b is built as standalone projection functions (dung_framework(&Model), grounded_extension(&AF)) rather than new Model fields, because the AF is a derived view of Model.edges for one consumer (the solver), not document data — compose, don't mutate.
rationale: Spec Decision 1: 'The AF is a derived view of Model.edges for one consumer (the solver), not document data. So: fn dung_framework(&Model) -> ArgumentationFramework ... The Model stays the parsed-document model; the AF/extension is a computed query. (Compose, don't mutate.)'

content: grounded_extension is implemented as a total characteristic-function least-fixpoint (no Result): all-UNDEC start, promote to IN when all attackers OUT / OUT when any attacker IN, iterate to a no-change pass, leftover stays UNDEC; HashMap-keyed state with unwrap_or(UNDEC) keeps lookups total for hand-built AFs with phantom attackers.
rationale: Implementation uses u8 state consts (UNDEC/IN/OUT), a `loop { for arg ... if !changed break }` fixpoint, and `state.get(a).copied().unwrap_or(UNDEC)`. Agent chose totality (no Result) because 'the grounded labelling is unique and always exists.'

content: Review rigor was scaled to risk: B6a (mechanical) got a single review pass, while B6b (the cross-cutting capstone) got a two-stage spec-compliance + code-quality review specifically tasked to scrutinize the fixpoint's correctness rather than trust the tests.
rationale: For B6a the agent ran one general-purpose reviewer ('mechanical slice — single reviewer suffices'); for B6b it dispatched two reviewers in parallel, instructing both to 'reason about whether it computes the least fixpoint (grounded) vs some other complete labelling' and 'don't just trust the tests.'

content: The reviewers verified the in-place (non-double-buffered) fixpoint is order-independent and computes the unique grounded labelling: transitions are monotone (only UNDEC→IN/OUT, never reversed), so stale intra-pass reads only defer decisions and never produce a wrong label; termination follows from the monotonically shrinking UNDEC count.
rationale: Code-quality reviewer: 'Stale intra-pass reads are harmless ... every promotion is monotonically justified ... A stale UNDEC read just defers a decision to the next pass; it can never cause a premature IN/OUT.' Both reviewers cross-checked 4-cycle and mixed-attacker cases against the live dung_extensions tool.

content: The agent reflected that 'probe, don't guess' resolved a debate pure reasoning could not: the skeptic's pipeline argument was internally coherent and would have led to a StatementMapper that silently diverged from the reference on every nested attack; one two-line probe turned it into a settled fact.
rationale: Final insight: 'The skeptic's pipeline argument was internally coherent and persuasive — it would have led to a StatementMapper that quietly disagreed with the reference on every nested attack. One two-line probe ... turned a confident architectural argument into a settled fact. The most dangerous designs are the plausible ones.'

content: Grounded the fuzzing setup in existing project conventions: edition 2024, resolver 3, no rust-toolchain file (stable by default, CI uses @stable throughout), and a reusable corpus-as-code in benches/parse.rs to seed from.
rationale: Agent after inspecting root Cargo.toml/CI/benches: 'I have the conventions: edition 2024, resolver 3, no rust-toolchain (stable by default — CI uses @stable throughout), and a reusable corpus-as-code in benches/parse.rs.'

content: Coverage-guided fuzzing (cargo-fuzz/libFuzzer) requires the nightly toolchain, which conflicts with the project's deliberate stable-only stance — the project had even chosen Criterion over nightly #[bench].
rationale: Agent identified the key fork: 'coverage-guided fuzzing needs nightly, but the project is deliberately stable-only (it even chose Criterion over nightly #[bench]). That's the key fork.'

content: Confirmed nightly (aarch64) and cargo-fuzz 0.13.1 are both installed locally, so the agent could fully build AND run the fuzzers to verify rather than only compile-check.
rationale: Agent: 'nightly (aarch64) and cargo-fuzz 0.13.1 are both available — so I can fully build and run the fuzzers locally to verify.'

content: Reading ast.rs, noted that Heading and Inference nodes (not just Statement/Argument/frontmatter) also carry optional Metadata, so the span-in-bounds oracle must walk those spans too.
rationale: Agent after Read of ast.rs: 'Confirmed the AST (note: Heading and Inference carry Metadata too — I'll walk those spans).'

content: Drew on the project ADR's record that span-correctness bugs (CRLF drift, char-vs-byte, record-before-whitespace) are the recurring defect class to justify an in-bounds span invariant as a high-value oracle beyond mere no-panic.
rationale: Spec context: 'The ADR also records that span-correctness bugs ... are the recurring defect class — so an in-bounds span invariant is a high-value fuzz oracle, not just no-panic.'

content: Chose oracles beyond no-panic for both fuzz targets — parse determinism, a whole-AST span-in-bounds invariant, and Dung AF/grounded-labelling well-formedness (attack endpoints are listed args; labelling partitions args) — to turn silent wrong results into crashes the search can find.
rationale: Spec decision 3 and target code: determinism asserts, check_document spans, and 'the grounded labelling partitions the arguments exactly once' assertions.

content: Made the fuzz/ crate its own workspace via an empty [workspace] table so the root workspace (members=crates/*) never compiles it, keeping the stable build/clippy --all-targets/test --workspace gate entirely nightly-free.
rationale: fuzz/Cargo.toml comment: 'An empty workspace table makes fuzz/ its own workspace, so the root workspace never compiles it — the stable build, clippy --all-targets, and test --workspace gate stay nightly-free.'

content: libFuzzer treats the corpus directory passed to 'cargo fuzz run' as WRITABLE and dumps generated inputs into it; pointing a run at fuzz/seeds/ polluted the committed seed set with ~3,810 generated files.
rationale: Agent: 'The fuzz runs polluted fuzz/seeds/ — libFuzzer treats the passed dir as the writable corpus and dumped generated inputs there.' git status showed thousands of A fuzz/seeds/<hash> entries; cleanup went from 3810 to 3 files.

content: After the seed-pollution incident, adopted a copy-seeds-into-gitignored-corpus run pattern and a .gitignore guard pinning seeds/ to *.argdown (seeds/* + !seeds/*.argdown) so a stray run can never commit generated inputs.
rationale: Agent edited .gitignore and run docs: 'guard against libFuzzer ever writing generated inputs into the committed seed set: only hand-written *.argdown seeds belong here'; run pattern copies seeds into fuzz/corpus/<t> instead of fuzzing seeds/ directly.

content: A PreToolUse security hook blocked the workflow write over command-injection risk; agent routed the matrix.target value through env: TARGET and referenced "$TARGET" rather than interpolating ${{ }} into run:, matching the project's CI discipline before re-issuing.
rationale: Hook error fired on .github/workflows/fuzz.yml; agent reasoned 'TARGET flows through env:, never interpolated into the shell, matching the project's CI discipline' and re-wrote with the safe env pattern.

content: Designed the seed corpus as three hand-written .argdown files — features (all grammar constructs + frontmatter + inline markup), dialectic (argument attack cycle), and pcs (multi-step premise-conclusion structure) — rather than committing binary fixtures.
rationale: Agent wrote fuzz/seeds/features.argdown, dialectic.argdown, and pcs.argdown each covering distinct construct coverage; spec notes 'one valid doc per construct + a mixed doc'.

content: The schemars JsonSchema derive used by the MCP tool types must match the exact schemars major version that rmcp depends on, or the build fails with a duplicate-schemars error.

content: argdown_core::Error carries public `message`/`offset` fields and is constructed cross-crate via a struct literal in the parser, so the fields must remain `pub`. The MCP tools rely on this to surface byte offsets in diagnostics.
rationale: Agent stated after reading parser lib.rs: 'Error lives in argdown_core with public message/offset fields (the parser constructs it cross-crate via struct literal, so they must be pub)', confirmed by parse() mapping e.offset() into Error { message, offset }.

content: dung_framework is a 'sharp' projection of the Model: nodes are arguments and the attack relation is exactly the argument→argument edges of kind Attack — statement-level attacks, supports, undercuts, and contradictories are excluded, matching @argdown/core's dung_extensions.
rationale: Agent read dung.rs whose module docs state the projection is sharp and excludes statement-level attacks, 'confirmed by probing'; agent then confirmed 'the dung signatures are confirmed' before writing the dung tool.

content: Enforce a boundary so only server.rs and main.rs import rmcp; tools.rs stays a pure core (&str → plain data) importing only the argdown_* crates plus serde/schemars, making all domain logic unit-testable without the protocol.
rationale: Plan File Structure section states 'Boundary discipline: only server.rs and main.rs import rmcp. tools.rs imports only the argdown_* crates + serde/schemars. Keep it that way.' and the architecture line describes a pure core wrapped by a thin rmcp boundary.

content: `parse` never returns a protocol error: it yields a ParseResult { ok, summary, diagnostic } even on malformed source, whereas export_model and dung_extensions map parse failure to ErrorData::invalid_params carrying the byte offset, and serialize failure to ErrorData::internal_error.
rationale: In tools.rs summarize returns ParseResult with Option<Diagnostic> ('Never an error' comment), while server.rs maps ToolError::Parse to ErrorData::invalid_params with json!({offset}) and ToolError::Serialize to internal_error.

rationale: Agent: 'I'll run a single reviewer that does spec-compliance first, then code quality (preserving the order and both dimensions while keeping dispatch count sane).'

content: Exactly one schemars version must exist in the dependency tree so the JsonSchema derive matches rmcp's; schemars 1.2.1 was already what rmcp 1.7.0 pulled, so no explicit pin was needed.
rationale: Task 1 report: 'schemars v1.2.1 was already the version rmcp pulled in, so cargo add schemars resolved to the same major and no pinning conflict arose'; cargo tree confirmed a single schemars version.

content: rmcp 1.7.0 server glue: the Parameters extractor lives at rmcp::handler::server::wrapper::Parameters (not the tool submodule); a unit-struct router compiles without a tool_router field; Json<T>/Result<String,ErrorData>/Result<Json<T>,ErrorData> satisfy IntoCallToolResult directly; and #[tool_handler(instructions=...)] is accepted as-is.
rationale: Task 5 implementer reconciled the rmcp 1.7.0 macro/import paths against the plan template via cargo doc and rmcp's test suite, reporting the actual use-lines and the working unit-struct pattern.

content: In rmcp 1.7.0 the stdio transport constructor is rmcp::transport::io::stdio, not rmcp::transport::stdio as the plan template assumed.
rationale: Task 6 report: 'use rmcp::transport::io::stdio;   // not rmcp::transport::stdio'.

content: Hypothesized that the non-zero exit with ConnectionClosed("initialize request") on empty stdin only occurs when no MCP handshake happens, so a real client would never hit it and the DONE_WITH_CONCERNS was acceptable.
rationale: Agent accepted the Task 6 concern: 'ConnectionClosed only fires when stdin closes before any MCP handshake (no real client) ... Task 7's in-process client will prove the real path works.' Later confirmed by the passing integration test.

content: rmcp 1.7.0 client API differs from the plan template: the call type is CallToolRequestParams (plural), built via CallToolRequestParams::new(name).with_arguments(map); a bare () implements the client handler; and the in-process test needs rmcp's client feature plus tokio's io-util.
rationale: Task 7 report: 'CallToolRequestParam → CallToolRequestParams ... ::new("name").with_arguments(map) builder pattern ... () already implements [ClientHandler]'; Cargo.toml gained the client + io-util features.

content: Confirmed the Dung projection semantics — child relation '-> <A>' under '<B>' means B attacks A, yielding B∈IN and A∈OUT — and cross-checked the local dung_extensions output against the live @argdown/core reference, which returned an identical partition.
rationale: Agent ran mcp__argdown__dung_extensions on the same source and got in:[B], out:[A], undec:[], noting 'Reference cross-check passes exactly ... identical to our dung_extensions.'

content: Discovered the per-task commits were not rustfmt-clean because formatting was only run at the final gate (by design), so cargo fmt --check at Task 8 surfaced accumulated diffs across server.rs, tools.rs, and integration.rs.
rationale: Agent: 'The gate caught formatting — the per-task commits weren't rustfmt-clean (fmt runs only at the final gate, by design).'

content: HMAC is unusable for this launcher because it is a symmetric MAC: verifying requires the same secret used to create it, so the secret would have to ship inside launch.mjs to every user, at which point anyone can forge a valid MAC.

content: The user's phrase 'HMAC with an RSA pair' conflates two incompatible primitives — HMAC (symmetric MAC) and RSA (asymmetric signature) — so the real question is whether to add a publisher signature for authenticity on top of the SHA-256 integrity check.
rationale: Agent: '"HMAC with an RSA pair" conflates the two; there's no construction that's both' and reframed it as 'do we want a signature (authenticity), not just a checksum (integrity)?'

content: SHA-256 here only provides integrity, not authenticity against a compromised source: the SHA256SUMS file is fetched from the same GitHub Release as the archive, so it is self-referential; TLS already supplies transport authenticity against MITM.
rationale: Agent: 'The checksum is self-referential — fetched from the same place as the thing it vouches for' and 'TLS already gives you transport authenticity'.

content: Discovered the planned e2e smoke step used `timeout 5`, which is unavailable on macOS by default; rewrote the step to rely on the MCP server self-terminating on empty stdin instead.

rationale: Plan note rewritten to: 'the staging dir is created under the cache base (same filesystem as the final location) so the publish `renameSync` is atomic — no cross-device (`EXDEV`) failure and no OS-tmpdir import needed.'

content: Judged the blast-radius 'scope may warrant splitting' decomposition flag to be a raw file-count heuristic rather than real coupling, since failure-impact fan-out was 0 and there were no cross-module edits.

content: Folded `email` into the marketplace owner / plugin author objects and added `type: stdio` to .mcp.json after a review found every real installed plugin manifest uses `email` (not `url`) and the comparable .mcp.json includes the stdio discriminator.
rationale: Reviewer evidence cross-checked against installed plugins (snowball, chrome-devtools, tool-executor); agent: 'two are backed by strong evidence that I'll fold in now to de-risk that validation.'

content: Verified that `node --test <dir>/` does not discover .mjs test files on Node 24 (directory form fails, glob form `*.test.mjs` passes 6/6), and corrected the plan's four test-command call sites to the glob form.
rationale: Implementer concern surfaced it; controller reproduced on node v24.16.0 ('=== dir form ===' fails, glob form prints 'tests 6 / pass 6 / fail 0') and edited the plan with replace_all.

content: Accepted a code-review finding that parseSha256Sums split on '\n', leaving a trailing '\r' on CRLF SHA256SUMS files that breaks the regex `$` anchor and silently returns null for every lookup; fixed the split to /\r?\n/ and added a CRLF test.
rationale: Agent: 'a CRLF SHA256SUMS leaves a trailing \r that breaks the regex $ anchor — every lookup returns null, making the launcher treat archives as unverifiable. In practice the file is LF ... but it's a latent bug in the security path.'

content: Accepted that die()'s process.exit(1) skips pending `finally` blocks, leaking the .tmp staging dir (including an unverified archive on attestation failure); changed the three in-staging failure sites to throw so the finally rmSync runs.
rationale: Reviewer (verified experimentally) found process.exit does not run finally; agent: 'leaking .tmp-* staging dirs (including an *unverified* archive on attestation failure). Fix: throw instead of die at the three sites inside the try.'

content: Accepted that re-raising a signal while the SIGINT/SIGTERM listeners were still attached made the launcher exit 0 instead of 130; fixed by removing the handlers (process.off) before re-raising so the default handler terminates by signal.
rationale: Agent: 'the signal re-raise doesn't remove the process listener first, so Ctrl+C makes the launcher exit 0 instead of 130 — wrong for a transparent proxy. Fix: process.off before re-raising.'

content: Adopted a rule to independently verify reviewer findings before acting in either direction — rejecting the reviewer's 'Critical' export_json rename (a false positive from the connected reference server) while accepting the @v1-stale finding.
